title: Logging
text: Pattern nine: logging on the hot path. A trading thread wants to log every fill. The general version formats and writes the line right there. The hot-path version copies a few numbers and moves on.

title: The general version
text: Here is what an assistant typically writes when the prompt states no latency budget. A logger with a mutex and an output file stream. Each call reads the clock, takes the lock, and streams the fields. Then std::endl flushes, so the line is on disk before the call returns. It is correct, thread safe, and easy to read. And all of it runs on the trading thread.

title: Where the time goes
text: Follow one call down to the machine. Reading the clock is cheap, a vDSO call with no syscall. The lock is an atomic read-modify-write, plus a futex syscall if another thread holds it. Each insertion is an out-of-line call that converts the number through the locale's num_put facet. Then the flush hands the buffer to the kernel: one write syscall per line. Compiled with -O2, this function is 106 instructions with 21 calls into the library, before the kernel starts.

title: The hot-path version
text: On the right, the hot-path version. The call fills a fixed 48-byte record in a single-producer, single-consumer ring. It checks a cached copy of the tail, so it rarely reads the consumer's cache line. It stores the raw time stamp counter, a pointer to the format string, and the raw arguments. One release store publishes the slot. If the ring is full, it drops and counts; it never blocks. That is 30 instructions and no calls.

title: Format later
text: The formatting still happens, just on another core. A background thread polls the ring, converts ticks to wall time, runs printf, and writes in 64 KB chunks. Arguments must be numbers or string literals, because only the pointer is copied. Size the ring and touch its pages at startup. A test checks that both versions write identical lines.

title: Measured
text: Measured on a shared 4-vCPU cloud VM, writing to a file, with a microsecond of work between calls. Median of five runs, hot thread pinned. The general logger takes 625 nanoseconds at p50, and 2.2 microseconds at p99. Swapping std::endl for a newline drops most syscalls: 261 and 1.2 microseconds. The ring takes 115 at p50, and 137 at p99. Most of that is one cache line moving between cores. That is 5 times faster at the median, and 16 times at p99.

title: The honest nuance
text: The bloat is not bad code. It comes from a missing constraint: this thread has a budget of nanoseconds and must never block. State that in the prompt, then measure. At startup, on config errors, and in tools, the simple logger is fine. Rule: on the hot path, log data, not text.
